name: LMP8640MKX-T_NOPB
title: Precision high-voltage high-side current sense amplifiers, fixed gain 20, 50 or 100 V/V
summary: LMP8640 and LMP8640HV measure the small voltage across a shunt resistor while its common-mode voltage sits anywhere from -2 V to 42 V (LMP8640) or -2 V to 76 V (LMP8640HV), and drive a buffered, ground-referred output. They run from a 2.7 V to 12 V supply. Each comes in three fixed gains, 20 V/V (-T), 50 V/V (-F) and 100 V/V (-H), with ±0.25% maximum gain error and ±900 µV maximum offset. LMP8640MKX-T/NOPB is the 42 V, gain-20 part in a 6-pin thin SOT-23 on a 3000-piece reel.
key_figures: -2 V to 42 V (LMP8640), -2 V to 76 V (LMP8640HV)

circuits.title: High-side current monitor driving an ADC
circuits.description: The shunt RS carries the load current from the load supply B1 to the load. +IN connects to the supply end of RS and −IN to the load end, so VOUT is the gain times RS × IS. The part runs from its own supply B2 (5 V to 5.5 V in the worked example), which also powers the ADC. RF and CF form a low-pass filter between VOUT and the ADC input. In the worked example the common-mode voltage is 48 V to 70 V, so the LMP8640HV is used; a 4.1 V ADC full scale at a 10 A peak with the 50 V/V option gives RS = 8.2 mΩ.

equations.name: Largest shunt
equations.note: At 10 A: 20.5 mΩ, 8.2 mΩ and 4.1 mΩ for gains 20, 50 and 100.

operation.text: Each input has an internal 4 kΩ resistor RIN. An error amplifier drives a MOSFET so the current through the +IN resistor makes its drop equal to VSENSE; that current, VSENSE / RIN, flows on through RG = 2 × RIN to ground, and an output stage of gain G (10, 25 or 50 V/V) amplifies the voltage on RG. Total gain is 20, 50 or 100 V/V. The output stage has low output impedance and needs no external buffer.

A larger shunt gives more signal against offset and noise, so better accuracy at small currents; a smaller shunt wastes less power at large currents. Input offset is usually what limits the smallest readable signal. The shunt must be rated above PD with margin for derating, and heat raises its resistance and shifts the reading; drift just after turn-on usually comes from shunt self-heating. Copper trace as a shunt has a tempco of 3300 to 4000 ppm/K (0.33% to 0.4% per °C), against 50 to 500 ppm/°C for a typical surface-mount sense resistor and 0.1 to 50 ppm for special low-tempco parts.

Connect the inputs to the shunt pads by Kelvin (4-wire) connections, not on the main current path, with identical trace paths so their errors cancel. Run the two traces together as a tight pair on one layer, away from digital, switching and motor lines, with clearance for up to 76 V. They carry only the bias current, about 12 µA per input at room temperature, so they may be thin. The +IN bias current rises by about VSENSE / 4 kΩ; the −IN current does not change with VSENSE. Unequal or large source impedances add error.

Any resistance in series with an input adds to the internal 4 kΩ and changes that input's gain, giving a fixed gain error; it also degrades offset and CMRR. Total trace resistance should stay below 10 Ω. Filter resistors, if used, must be equal on both inputs, and the gain then shifts slightly. External resistors are not a way to set gain.

operation.topic: Bias current at low common-mode voltage
operation.text: Below about +2 V common mode the input bias current reverses, crossing zero near +1.8 V; negative values are current leaving the inputs toward the load. The bias current figures are per input; the total is twice that and can reach 1 mA. Where a MOSFET switches a non-linear load (LEDs, a load behind a diode), this can hold the load above ground; bleeding it off takes a low-value resistor from the supply side of the load to ground.

The full common-mode range may be applied with V+ = 0 V. Unpowered, internal MOSFETs disconnect the RIN resistors and leakage is below 1 µA. The ±6 V differential limit still holds, and Zener clamps from the inputs to ground mean the absolute maximum input voltages still apply.

The output buffer can drive up to 30 pF or an ADC input directly. An RC low-pass at the output reduces noise and limits bandwidth. When V+ is above the ADC supply, a series resistor and a clamp diode to the ADC supply protect the ADC input, since transients and faults can push the output above its calculated maximum.

Requirement: 10 A peak, 10 mA resolution, 0.5% accuracy, 10-bit ADC with 4.1 V full scale, shunt below 10 mΩ, 48 V to 70 V common mode. The common-mode range calls for the LMP8640HV. Gain 20 would need 20.5 mΩ and is ruled out; gains 50 and 100 need 8.2 mΩ and 4.1 mΩ. The error budget shows 8.2 mΩ meets both resolution and accuracy; it dissipates 820 mW at 10 A.

Inputs work at common-mode voltages above V+: V+ can be 5 V while the monitored rail is up to 76 V. A bypass capacitor of typically 0.1 µF must sit as close as possible to V+ and ground for stability, with a voltage rating of 2× or more the highest applied voltage. Noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more decoupling. A series resistor at the output is advised for any capacitive load: cables, long traces, multiplexers, ADC inputs.

Use Kelvin connections to the shunt and keep load current out of the sense traces. Keep clearance round the input traces, which may sit at up to 76 V. Route the two input traces together on one layer; any vias should be continuous plated copper, and jumpers and connectors should be avoided, or matched in number on both inputs, since each junction is a thermocouple. Keep the amplifier away from heat sources and fast air flow, with equal copper on both input pins and both inputs equally far from any heat source. Give the shunt as much copper as possible to spread its heat. Place the 0.1 µF bypass right at the supply and ground pins.
